utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. First of all, I would like to apologise for having made everyone wait, but we had technical problems. Therefore, we are starting with approximately a 15-minute delay. I would like to, first of all, greet Mr. Zvonko Vidovic, who will take the affirmation in a few minutes. I would like to greet Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Pusic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Prlic, and Mr. Coric. I would like to greet Ms. West, Mr. Scott, as well as their associates, Defence counsel, and all the people assisting us. Before I ask Mr. Vidovic to read the solemn declaration, I will give the floor to the Registrar, who has two IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 3D has submitted its response to the Prosecution's objections to its documents tendered via Witness Milivoj Petkovic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01227. And 5D has also submitted its list of documents tendered through Witness Pero Nikolic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01228. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Witness, are you able to give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Vidovic. The 1st of October, 1963, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm the director of a private enterprise, a catering enterprise in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us your first name again, please? It's not on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before a court of law on those events that unfolded in the former Yugoslavia or are you testifying for the first time today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified in the County Court in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it a case related to the events that occurred in the former Yugoslavia or was this for another reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the trial against Dzidic et al, having to do with the war in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So you may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just some information by way of explanation. You will be testifying today, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. This is what has been scheduled. We are sitting this afternoon. Tomorrow morning, we will be sitting in the morning. On Wednesday, we will be sitting in the morning also. And on Thursday, we will be sitting in the afternoon. That said, on Thursday afternoon we shall finish at 6.00 p.m. You have just taken the affirmation, which means now that you are a witness of the Court, which means that you may not have any contact whatsoever with Mr. Coric's Defence team. In addition, you should not discuss with anyone the contents of your testimony, and you must not discuss this with the media either. Please try and be accurate when you answer the questions that are put to you. You will have to answer questions which Mr. Coric's Defence counsel will put to you. She will show you a series of documents. The other Defence counsel will intervene when the time comes to defend the other accused. I believe the Prosecutor - this will be Ms. West - will then cross-examine you. The three Judges sitting before you will also put questions to you. Normally speaking, we are four, but Judge Mindua is not here with us today because he is sitting in the Tolimir trial. Sometimes some of the Judges attend two cases on the same day. That will be my case tomorrow. If there is something which you do not understand, please don't hesitate to ask the person who has put the question to you to rephrase it, even if it is a Judge. This is what I wish to share with you to make sure that this hearing unfolds smoothly. I would like to greet Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic once more and give her the floor. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everybody else in the courtroom. Examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, too, Mr. Vidovic. I'm going to start off by asking you to speak up a little louder than when you answered the first few questions so that the interpreters can hear you. And the second thing I'm going to ask you is to speak slowly and make pauses between my questions and your answers. That is to help the interpreters, because all these proceedings are being interpreted into two languages. I'm going to read out a short biography, your CV, with respect to your activities in the HVO. And when I've read it all out, I'm going to ask you whether what I've read out is correct. In 1992, you were a student at the Faculty of Law in Sarajevo, and you lived and worked in Mostar at the same time as a private entrepreneur in the catering business. At the beginning of the war, you became a member of the 3rd Battalion of the HVO of Mostar. You were wounded in July 1992, and until October 1992, you were undergoing treatment. In October 1992, you became an operative in the Crime Prevention Department of the Mostar Police, and you remained in that post until the summer of 1993, when you became the head of the Crime Department in the 5th Battalion of the Military Police of Mostar. While you headed that department, you underwent professional training at the Faculty of Crime Sciences in Zagreb. At the beginning of November, 1993, you became the acting head of department, of the Crime Military Police Department, in the Military Police Administration. And in mid-December 1993, you left the military police and continued working in the catering business. Is everything I have read out correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My questions, Mr. Vidovic, will focus, for the most part, on your activity in the Crime Department in the Mostar section in 1993. To start off with, tell us how the Crime Prevention Department of the Military Police was organised in 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, the Military Police Crime Department, which is the department I worked in, was within the composition of the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police in Mostar, and later on, after July, the 5th Battalion of the Military Police in Mostar. The military police otherwise had five military police battalions. So in addition to the 1st, the other four had crime departments within them, under them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, these military police battalions, including your department, did they cover an operative zone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My job in the 3rd Battalion, and later on the 5th Military Police Battalion, was in the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now, tell us, please -- from your CV, we were able to see that you were first an operative in the Crime Department. Can you tell us what that means? What does an operative do?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an operative in the Crime Department of the Military Police, headquartered in Mostar, where I worked, my exclusive job was to uncover crime in the area covered by the Crime Department that I worked for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We saw that you were head of department for a time, or sector, in the Central Mostar area. So tell us what the head of the sector does. What's his job?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The head of sector does similar or almost identical work like the Crime Department operative, but with the added responsibility of conducting analyses and following the work of the entire department, which is made up of a number of operatives, until a criminal report is filed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a short time, you were the acting head of the Crime Department in the Military Police Administration. So what does the head of this department do?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The head of the Crime Department of the Military Police Administration is the man co-ordinating all the crime departments and involves analytical work. It is a post which dovetails and co-ordinates all the work and analyses the work of all the departments in the various battalions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the head of the Crime Department, does he give you any guide-lines or professional advice and things like that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as guide-lines and instructions, while I was working in the Mostar department we did receive those from the head of the Crime Department of the Military Police Administration. He would give us all the professional assistance we needed, ranging from what the various forms and documents looked like and anything else that we needed and that was involved in our work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were an operative in the Crime Department of Mostar, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: While I was working as an operative in the Central Mostar Crime Department, my immediate superior was Josip Marcinko, and he was the head of the Crime Department of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the immediate superior to this gentleman, Mr. Marcinko; who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His immediate superior was the battalion commander to which we belonged. And as I said a moment ago, I belonged, first of all, to the 3rd Battalion and then the 5th Battalion of the Military Police of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the commander's name? The commander of the 3rd Battalion, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Military Police Battalion in Mostar -- well, we had a situation in which until sometime in mid-April, the commander was Zeljko Dzidic, but after that he was replaced and Zarko Juric came to replace him. Later on, instead of Zarko Juric, it was Ivan Ancic, when the 3rd Battalion became the 5th Battalion under the reorganisation system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which post Zeljko Dzidic occupied after he ceased to be the 3rd Battalion commander, as you said, in mid-April sometime? Do you know where he went afterwards, that is to say, from mid-April onwards?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. All I do know is that from mid-April he was suspended because of some problems he had with some soldiers from Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Vidovic, do you know who was the superior to the commander of the 5th Battalion or 3rd Battalion? Who did he receive his orders from for daily tasks and assignments to be undertaken by the 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All the orders and assignments given to the 3rd Military Police Battalion, which was later the 5th Military Police Battalion, all the orders were received from the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who did you receive daily orders from?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had a system of daily briefings in the military police or the command of the -- or, rather, at the headquarters of the Military Police Battalion, and our head of department would attend those briefings. And then we would receive the daily orders that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that the 5th Battalion received orders from the South-East Herzegovina Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After I was given the duty of being at the head of the Military Police Crime Department for Mostar, I attended those daily briefings, and we would all together be given assignments, our daily assignments from the sphere of the Crime Police Department's remit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you how do you know. Did you hear that at the briefings? Was it at the briefings?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We would be given guide-lines at the briefings of the operative zone, assignments as to what the Crime Police Department was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what those orders were? What did they involve, what did they look like? Did you go about your regular duties without those orders as well during your daily work? So how was that different to the orders you received?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as those orders are concerned, yes, we did have our daily responsibilities and duties as a department. But then you also had orders which frequently involved us, as a department, for extraordinary situations and extraordinary tasks and assignments, because the commanders of the units who had problems with their soldiers would, through the operative zone, hand down to us certain matters that we were supposed to deal with within the crime department that we belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get an order to go to the front-line?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At a certain point in time when the security situation in Mostar was complex - I believe it was in July 1993 - we'd received an order for our department to provide a certain number of staff who would go to the first line in Mostar on the Bulevar. We went to the so-called Suma building, where we provided additional manpower to those on the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did you receive that order?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We received it from the Zone of Operations of South-East Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Vidovic -- just a minute. Let me see where we stand. To who did you report?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The system of work of our service was based on the practice that at the end of working hours - we worked from 8.00 until 4.00 p.m., but sometimes we stayed on until 9.00 p.m. - we submitted reports to the head of our centre, and then we would -- and all these reports of ours would be sent down. I'm saying "down" because we're one floor up. And these would then go to the operative zone. These would be reports about everything we had done on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the battalion sent its reports to the Military Police Administration too?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Military Police Battalion sent its reports to the Military Police Administration, and later on they were also sent to the command of the defence of the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that the battalion forwarded your reports to the zone of operations?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know because I would find out in my subsequent work. I would learn that the reports were, indeed, forwarded because I could see that link in the individual criminal cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you see that link? Did anyone contact you? Please explain for everybody to understand. What kind of link was it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As we worked with military personnel, we had constant contact with the commanders of the units, and that can be seen in our reports, where all this information flowed together and resulted in criminal reports. If a certain soldier from a unit was dealt with in a report, for example, it became clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My questions so far have been about the organisation of work and the mechanism of commanding in your sector. Do you know anything about the organisation of the military police in general, the system of command and control, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't really study the structure of the military police on the whole. I knew the structure of the department to which I belonged, and I stuck to the hierarchy in place; that is, the structure of the battalion of which I was part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you have no knowledge about what I had asked you about?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at the second document in your binder. You have two red binders, numbered binders. Take binder number 1, please. The second document is P00588.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me what the meaning of the Post-Its is? On some documents, you've written down some figures with exhibit numbers, and on the other documents there's nothing at all, or on the other Post-Its there's nothing at all. What does this mean? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all documents are marked, only some documents are very large, especially the first one, so possibly that made you think that it isn't marked, that it has no label.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't answered my question. I would like to know whether all the documents have already been admitted. If, on the other hand, some have not been admitted, I would like you to flag these up for me. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will mention every time which document has the status of exhibit, although the lower -- rather, the left corner of the document indicates its status. However, only the original documents have this mark of "EXH." There was a chart included, though, which also indicates the status of the document. But whenever I call up an individual document, I will mention its status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you this question because, as you know, sometimes the Trial Chamber dismisses some documents because they are not relevant. I feel that a counsel that has been working on this case for four years, if the counsel is presenting this document, that means that this document is relevant. I shall pay particular attention to the documents that might not be relevant to check whether there is a relevant association. If I don't say anything, that means I feel that it is relevant. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you told us a minute ago that it was your job to uncover crimes, or, rather, the perpetrators. And now take a look at document P00588, which is the Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and Article 137 is of interest to us here. In the English version, that's on page 0030-0164. This document has the status of exhibit already. In the Croatian version, that's on the page marked "0026-7327." Mr. Vidovic, please focus on me. You don't have to search. We'll take a look at the last paragraph of this article, which reads: "The armed forces include military police who take charge of security in military traffic, of military order and discipline, and the elimination of criminal elements in the armed forces." I suppose that this should have included criminal offences. Was it, indeed, your job to deal with criminal offences? I'm referring to the Crime Department of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was the job of the Crime Department to uncover criminal offences in the armed forces, but I must add something very important. For the Crime Department of the Military Police to uncover a criminal offence, we must first receive information about it. And pursuant to that information, we could start working and file a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your work as an operative of the Crime Department, which laws and regulations did you abide by?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The regulations that we abided by in our work, as operatives of the military police, were the following: The Law on Criminal Procedure and the Decree on District Military Courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, did you need the entire Law on Criminal Procedure for your work or did only a part of that law pertain to your work?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In our work, we only relied on the pre-criminal procedure. That is the part that we needed in our work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also use or abide by some material regulations that qualified criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We relied on the Penal Code of the former SFRY and the Penal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Why did you rely on both these pieces of legislation?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the simple reason that the Penal Code of the former SFRY dealt with more severe crimes, such as war crimes or crimes involving narcotics and the like, whereas the Penal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina dealt with all other criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir -- you told us that you relied on the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Decree on District Military Courts. Please take a look at the first document in your binder now, which is 4D01105. In the English version, this is on page 42, and we were looking at Article 151. This is the Law on Criminal Procedure which is an exhibit in this trial. Let us take a look at paragraph 1 of Article 151. I'll read it out slowly: "If there are grounds to suspect that a criminal act that is prosecuted ex officio has been committed, the law enforcement agencies must take the steps necessary to locate the perpetrator of the criminal act, to prevent the perpetrator or accomplice from hiding or fleeing, to direct and preserve the traces of the criminal act and objects which might serve as evidence, and to gather all information which might be of use to effectively conduct criminal proceedings." Tell us, Mr. Vidovic, did you apply this provision in your work? Was this provision pertinent for your activity?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As we were in war or in a state of immediate threat of war, we applied a provision of the Decree on District Military Courts, whereas this provision you've just read out was implemented by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please take a look at the third document in your binder, which is P00592. This is the Decree on District Military Courts. It is also an exhibit already. Please take a look at Article 6 which reads: "District military courts shall try criminal acts committed by military personnel and certain criminal acts committed by other persons as determined in this decree." Are you familiar with this provision, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the very provision I was referring to a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To which persons does the Decree on District Military Courts pertain?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To military personnel, that is, soldiers of the HVO, of which I was one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please take a look at Article 25 of this same decree. In the second paragraph of Article 25, we read: "District military courts shall perform the duties and exercise the authority as stated in the Law on Criminal Proceedings, of regular courts of the first instance." Could you tell us, please, who the authorised persons of the organs of security of the armed forces were?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If we take a brigade to represent the armed forces, the authorised person within the -- a brigade would have been the SIS of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please take a look at Article 27 now. Before I read it out, let me remind you that a short while ago we were looking at Article 151 of the Law on Criminal Procedure, and you said that it applied to civilians rather than military personnel and that the military police was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] I'm going to ask my question again. Every time I have an important question to ask, it never works. That's very strange. In any case, I'm still on Article 6. And I'm speaking to someone with a legal background, so I'm sure you will understand my question. This Article 6 is talking about military district courts. According to the text, those district courts are competent for military staff, and they will also try for criminal acts committed by other persons as determined in this decree. So I will choose a very simple case, and perhaps you can tell me who or which court would try in this case. Let's assume that we have a group of individuals wearing military uniforms, but we do not know to which unit they belong. This group of individuals will commit a certain number of crimes, and to be more precise, they will commit some rape. According to you, who would be in charge of the investigation of the inquiry as well as of sentencing of those individuals? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but the witness has just received the wrong interpretation in his head sets. He heard "if persons are military persons." All -- your question stated "wearing military uniforms," and I think that was the essential point of your question and it was interpreted wrongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm asking the interpreters to be very careful when translating my questions, which are always very important. And they are of a legal nature, so if there is the wrong interpretation, then, of course, we could come up with serious issues. So I would like to point out, Witness, that this group of individuals wear military uniforms, but we do not know if they belong to a military unit. So what I would like to know is whether they fall under Article 6 of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give this answer to your question. It will be a little longer answer. While I was in the Military Police Crime Department in Mostar, the concept of individuals wearing uniforms is very broad. So a person wearing a uniform does not necessarily mean that they belong to a unit and that they have a valid ID stating which unit that person belongs to. Now, if it has been established that the person does, indeed, belong to a unit, then, as a member of that unit, a criminal report is filed to the competent Military Prosecutor's Office. If he is a civilian wearing a uniform and has committed a crime which comes under the remit of the corresponding military district court, then it is that court which is in charge of conducting proceedings, if the crime is a serious crime like the one that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I don't know whether the interpretation was correct. You said: "If, as a civilian, he committed a crime from the remit of the court." Did you mean the acts listed under Article 7 of that same decree?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely those acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's look at Article 27 of this decree. And I'd like to remind you that when looking at the Law on Criminal Procedure, Article 151 there, well, I'd like to remind you that we've already seen that article and you said that this was applied to civilians and that it was linked to the provision with respect to military persons, and that in that case you applied Article 27, if it's applied to military persons. Now, we saw that the organ of internal affairs was duty-bound to apprehend the perpetrator, secure the traces, and so on. Now let's look at what Article 27 has to say, and I'm reading para 1: "The commander of a military unit and of a military institution must take all necessary measures to prevent the perpetrator of a crime under official prosecution from hiding or escaping, and must attempt to preserve all the traces of the criminal act and all objects that may serve as evidence. He must also obtain all information relevant to the criminal proceedings." Tell me now, please, when you said earlier on that you didn't apply Article 151 and the Decree on Military District Courts, did you have in mind this particular article?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I had Article 27 in mind of the Decree on Military District Courts, where it is specifically stated that it is the commander of a military unit who is duty-bound to take steps against a perpetrator, which means that every commander of a military unit, from a platoon upwards, is duty-bound to take all the necessary steps if one of his soldiers commits a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mean "all necessary measures," you mean the measures set out in this article; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Article 151 that we looked at earlier on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. I would like to go back to Article 27. The second paragraph, I believe, is important, Witness. When I look at this paragraph, it seems that the commander of a military unit, let's say the brigade commander, when he hears of a crime, he has to inform the district military prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm asking you this question, sir, because unfortunately General Praljak is not here. General Praljak is boycotting this trial at the moment. But had he been here, I would have asked the same question to you, but I'm sure his counsel will put the question to him as well. General Praljak, when he testified, he was in your seat, and I put to him that as a commander of the HVO, when a military commander gets to know of a crime, I was wondering what he should do. And I went into details by asking him whether he was not duty-bound to inform the prosecutor, and he had answered the following. I do not have the transcript, but I can recollect what he said. He said that, As long as the SIS or the military police is informed, then my role will stop there. So what do you think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll give a very categoric answer and say that the consistent application of Article 27, that is to say, that the commander of a military unit -- every commander of a military unit is obliged to take steps when he learns of a crime, and he is obliged to act according to Article 27, as is set out here. Now, if we're dealing with combat units or the front-line, then he would have to act in the same way as if it was a soldier of his who might have been somewhere outside the combat zone. That is to say that upon learning of a crime, he must secure the site, using two of his soldiers, and undertake all the other necessary steps which come under his authority, to secure the traces, prevent them being destroyed and so on. If the perpetrator was known to him, then he could file a criminal report straight away with the competent military prosecutor's office. If the perpetrator or perpetrators were unknown, then he could have informed us in the Crime Department so that we could then take the necessary steps to apprehend the perpetrators, because there are a lot of professional work -- there's a lot of professional work involved. But it was up to the commander of a military unit to secure the site where the crime had taken place and to take all the other necessary steps under Article 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you clarified the situation. I would like to thank you. You have just said, and it's important, if the unit commander does not know the identity of the perpetrators, and that was one of the cases put forward by General Praljak, and you just said it, in that case he has to inform the Crime Department and he has to inform the military police. Very well. But in case you do not do anything, let's assume that you are not taking any steps, what should the military unit commander do in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hypothetically speaking and hypothetically looking at this situation, then what we would do was to file a criminal report against perpetrators unknown, as far as we are concerned, if we'd been informed of a crime having taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where would you file this report, before which structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the District Military Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My apologies for asking basic questions to you, but the answers have to be in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, one detail that I'd like to focus on. You quoted my client's position correctly, and the witness has answered with the explanation given, but I'd just like to remind you that those questions were asked of my client earlier on precisely with respect to Article 27, and he was -- the article is lex specialis, regulating a special situation; that is to say, when the perpetrator's caught red-handed, in flagrante, so when the perpetrator is known. The moment a crime took place, somebody knew that the crime had taken place and knew who the perpetrator was, that's one procedure, and the witness said that. The situation is different if the perpetrators are unknown. Then it's not this article that applies, but other principles. So here we know that a crime has -- or, rather, when we know that a crime has been committed, but not the perpetrators, then the other organs come into play. So as you are dealing with the crux of the matter, bear in mind that Article 27 is lex specialis. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have nothing against Mr. Kovacic giving us legal expertise, but I think that the witness is here to answer that and not to have Defence counsel interpret what something means, particularly not at this stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, anyway, Witness, I'm going to ask you again. You said -- you uttered a sentence a moment ago to this effect: You said that if a commander does not know who the perpetrator is, then he will call upon you. Tell me now, if he does not know who the perpetrator is, does he still have to undertake steps under Article 27, if the perpetrator is unknown, that is to say, to secure the site of the crime and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as he learns of a crime being committed, regardless of the perpetrators are known or unknown, it is his duty to apply Article 27 and act upon it, that is to say, to use his soldiers to secure the crime scene, to try and secure all the traces and any objects that might be used in evidence, and carry out all the other steps which, conditionally speaking, would help us in our job later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us now, in what way does he inform you -- does the commander inform you of a crime and that he needs your assistance? How would he do that, regardless of whether it's a crime for which he does not have the professional capacity to deal with it or that they need to uncover the perpetrator? Anyway, what is the manner in which he informs you? How does he do that, how does he inform you of a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All information about a crime is received by us from the commander and from the military police battalion to which I belonged with my crime department, and the battalion received it from the operative zone that we were located in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, according to Article 27, was the commander authorised to apprehend and arrest an individual that he considered was the perpetrator of a crime?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He certainly did have the authority to arrest an individual immediately if that individual had committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you look at paragraph 4 of that same article, Article 27, which reads as follows: "The military commander, as company commander, whose status is equal to or higher than that of a commander of the company or an authorised official person working for the internal affairs and the security organs of the military police, may arrest a member of the military in cases which have been determined by the Law on Criminal Proceedings on detention." Tell us, please, do you know whether this was the way things worked?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this military commander occupying the post stipulated under Article 27 could arrest a suspect, just as a policeman from the Ministry of the Interior could do, and just as an operative from SIS could do, and just as a military policeman could do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have just seen that you could have been informed about the commitment of a crime by the commander, and you said that such information is required for you to be able to work. But what were the other ways for you to receive information about crimes committed? What was it like in practice?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We got information from citizens directly. They came to our department in Mostar frequently and reported various crimes to us, which shows that they trusted us. And we were informed by the police station or the Police Administration of Mostar; in other words, the MUP. We were also informed by the permanent patrols of our battalion of the military police which patrolled Mostar day and night, and also from the commanders just mentioned, so we had various sources of various types of information about crimes committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you learned of the commitment of a serious crime, what did you have to do? Let's take murder as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Before we get to this question, which is very interesting, I'm still on paragraph 4 of Article 27. I'm going to use a case. I like cases or examples, because through examples we can actually clarify some issues. Let's take a hypothetical example. Let's assume that a brigade commander learns that one of his men is going betray the unit by deserting, and this could be a potential threat for the entire unit because the brigade commander has enough reasons to think that this soldier has joined enemy ranks. According to you, do you think that the unit commander can arrest this soldier and disarm this very soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he can arrest and disarm him. As brigade commander, he has an assistant for the SIS and there is also military police in the brigade. The example you mentioned has repercussions on security. So the commander would contact his assistant for SIS to conduct preliminary activities before arresting the soldier, if indeed the soldier is planning on deserting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Article 27 states that in this case, the suspect has to be led within 12 hours -- or be taken within 12 hours before an investigating judge of the District Military Court. Would this mean that a suspect arrested by the unit commander, or by someone from the SIS, or by someone from the military police, does that mean that the suspect has to be taken before an investigating judge of the District Military Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had a dead-line of 12 hours to inform the investigating military judge on the reasons for detention. The investigating military judge gave us permission, by an order of his, for an additional 72 hours in case, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Last question, and please listen carefully. Let's have a case where we have arrested someone who was about to betray a unit, but this person is not brought before an investigating judge within 12 hours. According to you, in which situation do we find ourselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer this question. I believe I would have to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Vidovic, now that the Judge asked you about these 12 hours and 72 hours, this applies to police detention while you are conducting investigative measures; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is when we conduct investigative measures in relation to the suspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period of time, if you conclude that you have no proof that that person is, indeed, the perpetrator, or if the time-period elapses without you establishing that he's a perpetrator, do you have to release him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that person is no longer interesting to us from the aspect of the Crime Department of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were now speaking about police detention. Can the investigating judge order a certain person to be detained? I'm now speaking about placing someone in remand prison.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the investigating judge can do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even after the 72 hours have elapsed?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what the longest time-period was, under the Law on Criminal Procedure, for somebody to remain in remand in accordance with the -- or pursuant to an order of the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to speculate. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you a question, but you had no time to answer, so I'll go back to it now. If you should have found out that a serious crime has been committed, such as murder, what would you be duty-bound to do? Did you have to inform anyone?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: After receiving information about the crime of murder, we had to inform the district military prosecutor immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In such cases, does the investigating judge participate? And if so, how?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating military judge takes part in the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we have heard what you were informed about and what you did in case of a serious crime. So once you have information, what do you do next?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Crime Department of the Military Police then takes all necessary measures from our jurisdiction in order to carry out all preparations that come before a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you be more specific or give us some examples of something that you did?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So we collect all objects that can be used as evidence, the traces of the commitment of the crime. We conduct interviews and make official notes about them. We all take statements from persons interviewed or persons who could provide useful information. And then we use all that material for the drafting of a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once a criminal report is drafted, to who do you submit it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When a criminal report has been drafted, a person from our department, who was in charge of drafting criminal reports, submits them to the District Military Prosecutor's Office in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you submit that criminal report, you have found the perpetrator and submitted the report to the Military Prosecutor's Office, do you still have any obligations with regard to that case or is that case completed from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: By submitting the criminal report to the Prosecutor's Office, our job is done. But it happened very often that while working on another case, we learn of some facts relevant for the other case, and we submit -- we inform the Prosecutor's Office of that, too, as an addendum to that previous criminal report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can the public prosecutor request additional information from you or ask you to conduct certain activities subsequently?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It happened very often that the public prosecutor requested some additional activity from us, and we would certainly respond to those requests whenever we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the prosecutor request such information from other persons as well, other services?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since our service was poorly equipped, from the point of view of technology, the prosecutor may have requested forensic assistance from the MUP or assistance from military commanders to collect information about the person in question, if that person was a member of a certain military unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask you a question which may prove useful once we deliberate. You just said someone prepares the report which is to be forwarded to the military prosecutor, and then that's where your work ends, unless additional information is provided, which you will then forward to the military prosecutor. Fine. What I would like to know is this: Please listen carefully. When the report is drafted for it to be sent on to the military prosecutor, do you always ask for permission from the military unit commander whom the soldiers belong to or don't you ask him anything whatsoever; you simply forward the report to the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, Your Honour, you mean that I seek permission to submit a criminal report to the Prosecutor's Office. If so, the answer is, no, I never did that. We were autonomous in all matters with regard to the -- to criminal reports. We were a sort of service of the public -- of the Military Prosecutor's Office and all our criminal reports went to them. We never applied to any military commander to allow us to submit our criminal reports to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you collected information and established the identity of the perpetrator of a crime, you know that the perpetrator is a soldier and member of a certain unit, were you duty-bound to inform his commander?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The daily reports that we drafted in our department at the end of working hours, if they included the information that a criminal report was filed against a soldier, it would be forwarded through the battalion of the military police up to the zone of operations, and we would inform the military commander of the fact that a criminal report was submitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the military commander of the unit whose member the perpetrator was?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you complete that stage of the investigation, you do everything necessary, but the identity of the perpetrator remains unknown. What did you do in such cases?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Unknown perpetrators, or "NN" as they were designated, would not be -- such cases would not be closed. We would never close NN cases. We would always strive to find information that could lead us to the perpetrator. After several months of work, doing something else altogether, we would often stumble upon information that we needed in the other case, and then we would file a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have fully understood which procedures apply to NN, non-identified perpetrators, and you've described to us in detail what happens when the perpetrator is identified. I shall now put to you a question. It is a shame that General Praljak is not here today. I hope that he will come back again soon. General Praljak had told us this: Listen carefully. He told us that, As a military commander, I hold a defence line facing the enemy. If I hear that among the soldiers on this defence line there are some that have committed offences, I shall not arrest them straight away, because if I arrest them, I will then weaken my defence line and the enemy can make a breakthrough in that case, which can prove disastrous for my defence. Therefore, I keep the soldiers in the unit, even though they have committed offences. I'm summing up what he has told us. What do you think of this? What do you think of this view, which has been given to us by the number-one man in the HVO at the time he was in this position? He told us that as far as he was concerned, there was no question of arresting the soldiers who had committed offences, in light of the fact that this would pose a threat on the defence line. What do you think of this theory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to speculate at a theoretical level. I'll just repeat what I said a short while ago. Working for the Department of the Military Police and strictly abiding by all the regulations, our task was to combat crime and find perpetrators of crime. That's all I can say to what you have just outlined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like us to clarify something. Tell me, please, did you file criminal reports about perpetrators unknown, NN?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly? You file a criminal report against perpetrators unknown, and then you continue to investigate and do your job. And if you uncover who the perpetrator was, then you make an addition to the criminal report and add the person's name and surname and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We always kept the investigation alive and the case alive until the perpetrators were uncovered. We would just add on and supplement the criminal reports filed. The first criminal report filed when we learned about a crime and sent to the military prosecutor, and then we would update it with new information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would like us to look at a separate set of documents which relate to uncovering -- well, the accused have drawn my attention to the time and that it might be a good idea to take the break. We did start later, but we're getting signals from that part of the courtroom. So before I move on, perhaps this would be a good moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, understandably so. These hearings are very long. We shall have a break, a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we look at the documents, tell us what the conditions were in 1993 in Mostar, and how did they affect your work? What was the situation like in the town of Mostar, and did it have any effect on your work?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the year?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, Mostar was a war zone. After the fighting stopped, the fighting that took place in the summer of 1992, there was a sort of interim situation which was neither war nor peace, and we tried to get back to normal, get life back to normal, at the beginning of 1993. And then in May 1993, in Mostar, the situation escalated and there was an armed conflict between the BH Army and the HVO, which made it a war zone again. There were a large number of refugees which had already come into Mostar in 1992, after the Serb aggression against parts of Eastern Herzegovina, and all this led to a situation in which we had a large number of refugees, and they were put up in collective shelters and accommodation, like the student hostels that used to exist before the war. And there were large stores selling white goods and the like, and they were transformed into places where the refugees could be put up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you at this point? Perhaps we could speed up a bit.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in addition to these refugees put up in collective accommodation, there were many flats that had been left empty during 1992, and these refugees took up residence there, which caused us a great deal of problems in our work, in my line of work, because we had no records about the people coming into Mostar and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what the situation was like with respect to the army. Were there many soldiers, military units, around; were they stationed there all the time or did they change locations; was there a lot of coming and going to and from Mostar, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the military is concerned, and a moment ago we mentioned the person who was a soldier only because he was wearing a uniform, the whole town was full of people wearing uniforms. We had different units coming into town and leaving a few days later. The army -- the soldiers were put up in barracks outside town, but also in the town proper. So as far as the army was concerned, the town was full of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, was it only members of the military units who wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody or almost everybody was wearing a uniform, some because they were members of a unit, others as camouflage, portraying themselves as being members of units. So the vast majority of people in town were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the situation like with respect to electricity, the public lighting system and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, during the war and the war operations, we were left without any electricity in [indiscernible], so throughout the war there was no street lighting. Flats would have electricity for a short while. It would come and go. So the situation was rather chaotic with respect to electricity and lighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A very short question, Witness, regarding the previous answer. You said almost everyone wore uniforms. Is that a gender-neutral answer? Does that include men and women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant men mostly, although not infrequently you could see women wearing uniforms too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, how were you technically equipped, you in the Crime Department?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the Crime Department was being formed - well, it started to be formed in 1992, sometime in October, when I arrived, it was in its inception - it was poorly equipped, and that applied to almost the whole of 1993, which meant that we did not have the necessary manpower or equipment to be able to do the job properly, so that we had to rely on people from the Ministry of the Interior very often who did have some equipment surviving from peace time. We were poorly equipped. We did not have enough cars, or equipment, or professionals, so, generally speaking, the service was poorly equipped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you have any forensic experts, pathologists, ballistics experts and the like?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We would go to the Ministry of the Interior for forensic services. And as for ballistics, our department at a point in time had very good co-operation with the ballistics experts from the Republic of Croatia. And I remember a gentleman called Catipovic [phoen] who was a ballistic expert, and we would send them our samples for expertise. But this process was a lengthy one. It would last four or five months and even as long as a year, because Croatia was also at war at that time and it was only from them that we could receive ballistic assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, court pathologists, people trained to conduct post-mortems. Did you have that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. We also had to rely on Split for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's take a brief look at the documents. Some of the documents that I'm going to show you are ones you've already seen during the proofing session. They're not from your operative zone, but I'm going to show them, nonetheless, because they are typical documents and you'll be able to tell us whether that was the type of document that you were familiar with. So let's look at the first one, which is P01405. It's not an exhibit yet. Can you tell us what kind of document this is? What is it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document which the 4th Battalion of the Military Police from Vitez compiled it, compiled a criminal report, sending it on to the military prosecutor in Travnik. So this, then, is a document which clearly shows how the Crime Department of the Military Police functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see here, after where it says "Criminal Report," then it says "against" and "because," and then it says that it is the crime of murder, that this concerns the crime of murder. And we can see that it was -- the crime was committed against Esad Salkic, the plaintiff. Now, what ethnicity was this person?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Esad Salkic was a Bosniak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next document, which is P01503. It's already an exhibit. It is from the Military Prosecutor's Office in Travnik, District Military Prosecutor's Office in Travnik. What is this?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It's a request to conduct an investigation. It's a continuation of something, and that is to say that something is a criminal report that was previously filed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says there are grounds to suspect that on such and such a day, due to an ethnic clash, Elezovic, Nermin, was killed, as was Sekovic, Jasmin. Now, these two persons, on the basis of their names, looking at their names, can you tell us what ethnicity they were?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: They were Bosniak Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document, which is P03513. It's still not an exhibit. It's a daily report for the 16th of July, 1993, of the 1st Company of the 1st Military Police Battalion of Mostar. And under the heading "Street Patrol Service," it says: "In the morning hours, a civilian policeman, Marin Vidovic arrived with a report linked to -- concerning two girls who were kidnapped the previous day in the street. After having being kidnapped, they were raped, mistreated, and then they were threatened not to say anything to anyone about it or else they would be killed. The above-mentioned civilian policemen told us the name of one of the perpetrators, and that was Mario Pazin. And since we were also informed that the perpetrators had the insignia 'VP,' we made a check in order to find out whether that man is a member of our company, and we found that he was a member of our unit." And it goes on to say that: "After this perpetrator was apprehended, the other perpetrators of this sordid crime were also apprehended." And then we see their names. I don't have to read them. Tell me, are you familiar with this event? Did you know about it, do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember. I was directly involved in the work of this criminal report that was filed, four members of the military police, and a criminal report was filed against these four members. They were convicted of the crime, and they were thrown out of the military police as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, do you happen to remember -- since two girls are mentioned here, do you remember what their ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think they were Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following on from what you've just said, you've looked at the documents, they all refer to the same case, so shall we go through them just briefly, and then you can tell me whether you remember the documents and what they were about. The first document that we're going to look at is P03483, and it's the record of an interview of Jadranko Ebrun [phoen], or Jadranka Ebrun. The following document is P03508. It's a report from your department, relating to the same incident. Then we come to a record of an interview, which is P03482, and we see that it is an interview of Mario Pazin, one of the perpetrators mentioned previously. And then we come to P03497, which is a form for prisoners' escort, with the names of the perpetrators. And, finally, number P03523, we have a criminal report from your department. Are you going to say -- tell us whether all these documents which we've looked through are ones that you are familiar with? And if so, what do they show?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, these documents and the sequence they are placed in show the way in which the service functioned, the service that I worked in. And we see in this document exactly what the order of our work is, regardless of whether it had to do with military policemen or any other soldiers of the HVO. I just wish to note that at the moment when we arrest these soldiers, they were working on the security detail of the president or something like that. However, they were military policemen and they were arrested, and criminal charges were brought against them, as we saw in the last document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether they were convicted?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at P03571. That's the next document. The first page is an authorisation, and the second page is a request. And on the third page, we see the photographs of these persons. It has to do with their eviction from the military police. You already mentioned that. Do you remember, were they thrown out of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were no longer military policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the next document now, P04143. This is a criminal report. We see that it is filed against unidentified perpetrators. You explained the procedure to us previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Before we look at the next document, I went through all the documents, like you did, and indeed you said that the four individuals were sentenced. We had already heard of that. We realised that they were members of the security team of Mr. Prlic, so they were in charge of Mr. Prlic's security. When you did your job, were you not prevented from doing your job, as part of the Crime Department, regardless of the position of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we did not have any obstacles in our path, because it had to do with some kind of security. For us, they were military policemen. You will see the sequence of these dates, how these things developed, that this was done in a very short period of time. The matter had to be dealt with urgently, and that's how we treated it. Again, I say that we filed a criminal report, and in this way we concluded our work in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as far as you can recollect, what sort of sentence was handed down for these four individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer that question. I really don't know what kind of prison sentence they were sentenced to, but I do know that they were sentenced. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are looking at document P04143. This is a criminal report that has to do -- actually, this is already an exhibit. I am bringing it up because we see, first of all, that it's against NN, unknown perpetrators, and we see there are nine individuals who are injured parties. And we see it's the village of Mokronoge, where the crime was committed. Tell me, please, on the names of these individuals, can you tell me what their ethnic background is?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All of them are Bosniak Muslims by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether you had heard of this case?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I had heard of this case. At first, it was dealt with by the Crime Department of the Military Police of Tomislavgrad, and a report was filed against perpetrators unknown. And later on, I also participated in dealing with this criminal report because we actually did receive some knowledge about the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, once you received this knowledge, was the perpetrator's name included in the report, and do you know what ultimately happened?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His name was inserted, Ivan Bakovic, nicknamed Ruda. I think that he is still serving his sentence. For a while, he was a fugitive, or, rather, he was a member of the 2nd Guards Brigade of the Croatian Army. After this crime, he sought shelter in Croatia, but he was later found there and arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he did in Livno as a member of the 2nd Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by his last name, I think that he originally came from that area. He may have been there on leave or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the next document, P06727.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Before we move on to the next document, I was looking at the description of the crime, and when I was a prosecutor, had I seen what happened here, I would have jumped on my seat, because when investigators arrive it says that UNPROFOR had moved the dead bodies. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not directly participate in that because I had worked in Mostar throughout. Livno is a different operations zone. It's quite simply a different zone. I just got involved when the identity was made known, and then I was engaged in the search for Mr. Bakovic. However, I cannot tell you about these details because I did not take part in that segment of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And as far as you know, did UNPROFOR intervene in the investigations that you would carry out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of any such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we are looking at document P06727. This is a criminal report from your department against a person by the name of Miroslav Kolobara. It is the name that matters. This report pertains to some of the problems that he created in the war hospital in Mostar. Do you remember this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I remember this incident, but by then I was already in Ljubusko and this matter was dealt with by Mostar. I do remember the incident, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the next document. That is 5D04168. Previously, when explaining the principle according to which you worked, you said that once you filed the report, and if you gained any additional knowledge, then you would -- then you would inform the Prosecutor's Office about that. 5D04169. We saw Miroslav Kolobara. Again, here we see "Miro Kolobara." Can you tell us what this is all about? Can you --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is precisely the addendum to the criminal report that was signed by Zeljko Covic, the then head of department. It was sent to the District Military Prosecutor's Office, so it had to do with some new knowledge that was acquired in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at 5D04168 now. It has to do with the same person, Miro Kolobara. However, now there is another person involved, another perpetrator. In the first document, we saw that it was a criminal report that pertained to some trouble at the hospital, and then we saw the addendum where there's a reference to Kemal Selimovic and Miro Kolobara, and now we see this request for carrying out an investigation against two persons, Miro Kolobara and Kemal Selimovic. And it says here, in the further text, because there are reasonable grounds to suspect that such and such had happened, he entered Drago Mijatovic's apartment, from which he brought out three men and a woman and a girl, all of Serbian ethnicity, allegedly. The accused then drove these individuals to the separation line near Staklena Banka and took them over to the left bank of the Neretva river. Tell me -- this is a request for carrying out an investigation. Can you give us your comments in this regard?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My only comment is that once we completed our work, the Military Prosecutor's Office did whatever was within the scope of their work. They carry out their assignments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, the person mentioned under number 2, Kemal Selimovic, it says here that he is a member of the HVO. And it says he's the son of Husein and his mother's name is Rabija. Can you tell us what his ethnicity was, judging by his name and surname?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He is a Bosniak Muslim. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Could we please look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. Witness, I was busy reading this document. Miro Kolobara is a member of the Convicts Battalion. This might be of importance. As for the second individual, Kemal Selimovic, son of Husein, would he not be a Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please repeat your question? I didn't quite understand it. Kemal Selimovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "son of Husein." Is he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's a Muslim, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So he is a Muslim. So they break into an apartment, and they are three residents of Serbian nationality. And if I understand correctly, this apartment is in West Mostar. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bijeli Brijeg 29 is in the west part of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And apparently those two individuals, who are members of the HVO and of the Convicts Battalion, those two individuals, they were saying, Bring those three people towards East Mostar, if I understand correctly. And then the military police has decided to launch an investigation on them and is going to arrest them; and the crime is committed in August 1993. So, Witness, as far as you know, was there in West Mostar a plan aimed at sending away Muslim or Serbian people to take them to East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only answer I can give is that this is an isolated case. I had never heard of any kind of plan akin to the one that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So as far as you're concerned, it's an isolated case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you have not heard of any other case of the sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know of other cases as well. However, as for the Kolobara/Selimovic case, I thought that that was an isolated case. That's what I meant. It wasn't part of a broader plan, as you had asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as you can recollect, Miro Kolobara, who, I believe, must have been heard by the investigators, what did he say exactly? Was he carrying out orders that had been given by his commander or did he say that he committed this crime for personal reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what he said. I wouldn't want to guess now. But I actually believe that it is a question of personal motives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is unfortunate that we didn't get the audition of Kolobara because we may get some additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... good thing to correct the transcript straight away. In line 19 - we still have it on our screen - your question that starts with: [In English] "And you have not heard of any other case of the sort ..." [Interpretation] What follows is actually the witness's answer, but it hasn't been separated that way in the transcript. So perhaps we should correct it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, you're very right. Very well, please proceed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lest there be any misunderstanding, when you said that this was an isolated case, did you mean that such actions were not planned or organised?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, such actions were not organised or planned. These are things that were committed by individuals, and we, in the department that I worked in, fought against that throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your work, did you deal with cases that involved evictions from apartments, forcible evictions, mistreatments? Did you come across such cases in your work?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We did have such cases. Citizens turned to us, they turned to our department every day. Citizens who faced such problems came and reported such matters to the military police. There was no obstacle in their path. They reported mistreatments and attempts to evict them from their apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you would receive such information from citizens, what would you do?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC
